title: Ask them first
hookLine: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs against God; wrongs against people need their forgiveness (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)

lines: ONE THING THE DAY WON'T DO.
cards: It's Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and a man has been in synagogue since the evening before. He's fasting, standing for the long prayers, beating his chest at every line of the confession.
And somewhere across town is his sister, whom he hasn't spoken to since a bad argument last spring. He's been thinking about her all day.
The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, has a sentence for exactly this man. The day he's keeping can do a great deal. But there's one thing it won't do for him.

teach.h: THE DAY ATONES FOR SOME WRONGS.
teach.b: First, the line. In the tractate on Yom Kippur, the Mishnah says it plainly: for wrongs between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones.
For wrongs between a person and another person, it does not atone, until the one who did wrong makes peace with the one they wronged. Second, where it comes from.
The Mishnah names Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, reading a verse from Leviticus about the day.
In the King James, the verse ends: "that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD." He reads those last words closely. Before the Lord.
The day cleanses what lies between you and God. What lies between you and your sister stays where it is until you go to her. Third, how far you have to go.
Maimonides, in his Laws of Repentance, makes it practical. You go to the person and ask.
If they refuse, you go back with others, a second time and a third. If they still refuse, you may stop, and now the one refusing carries the fault. The asking is required.
Fourth, why it matters. In the Mishnah's reading, God doesn't do your apologizing for you. The person you hurt isn't skipped over on the way to heaven.
And so, on the day before Yom Kippur, some Jews make a point of calling, writing, or knocking on a door.

how: Before Yom Kippur, some Jews seek out family, friends and colleagues to ask forgiveness directly, following the Mishnah's teaching that the day does not atone for wrongs against people until the person is reconciled.

o: a fast day that wipes away every kind of wrong
the Day of Atonement; wrongs to people need their peace first
the Jewish new year, when the ram's horn is blown

games.q: ask them first — tap the pairs.
p: reads the verse: before the Lord
go back a second and third time

s: the Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones for every wrong, whoever it hurt
for wrongs against another person, the day does not atone until you make peace with them.
Maimonides says to go back if the person refuses the first time
a second time and a third, with others; after that, the one refusing carries the fault.
in this teaching, the person you wronged must forgive you
the asking is required; the answer is theirs.

games.q: it's Yom Kippur. you've fasted and confessed all day, and you still haven't called your sister. by the Mishnah, where does that wrong stand?
o: the day has atoned for it.
it waits until you make peace with her.
games.why: the Mishnah says the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs against God, but not wrongs against a person until you make peace with them.

practice: Bring to mind one person you owe an apology who could actually hear it from you, and find the plain words: not the long explanation, not the reasons, just what you did and that you're sorry, in a sentence or two.
Say them to yourself until they sound true. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for the courage to go.

wordCard.voice: Yom Kippur. The Mishnah's teaching: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs against God, but wrongs against people need the person you wronged. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the answer is theirs. The asking is the part that's yours. Day nine hundred forty-two.
